newsitem.title: INDIA: Kissinger backs India bid for U.N. council seat.
newsitem.headline: Kissinger backs India bid for U.N. council seat.

text.p: India won support from former U.S. secretary of state Henry Kissinger on Saturday for its drive to become a permanent member of the U.N. Security Council.
Kissinger said India's growing economic and political power meant it deserved a seat on the U.N. council.
"I do think that India has a claim to a seat," he told a business conference in the capital New Delhi. "India will become a major player and play a significant international role."
Former Australian prime minister Paul Keating told the same gathering he no longer opposed India's membership in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.
"We can start to consider new members in APEC," Keating said, "and I can certainly see a role for India in that."

Kissinger, building on his familiar theme of the limitations of U.S. power, said the United States should not try to determine the outcome of a longstanding dispute between India and Pakistan over the Himalayan region of Kashmir.
"There are some issues where our (U.S.) contribution will be finite," he said. "It (Kashmir) is an issue that has to be dealt with between India and Pakistan."
India and Pakistan have agreed later this month to resume bilateral peace talks which broke down in 1994 over Kashmir.
The neighbours have fought three wars since independence in 1947, two of them over Kashmir which is divided between the two nations.
Kissinger said Washington should not try to force India or Pakistan to roll back their nuclear weapons capabilities, but to ensure that such weapons do not proliferate.
India exploded a nuclear device in 1974 but says it has ever built the bomb. U.S. experts believe both India and Pakistan could quickly assemble nuclear weapons.

Kissinger, who helped establish U.S. ties with China in the 1970s, said Washington should resist the temptation to "organise Asia on an anti-China basis" with an aim to curbing Beijing's growing influence.
"I think we should have a serious dialogue with China on proliferation, Korea, the world order," he said.
"The United States has no necessity in declaring any country in Asia an inherent enemy. It can afford to wait until an enemy appears and then judge."
Kissinger said he supported the expansion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) eastward to include some former communist countries, despite Russia's opposition.

But he said he felt the debate over NATO expansion was getting bogged down in "endless dialogue over technical military issues" and not focusing on the political problem of integrating Russia into the world community.
